lesson.grammar_point: gradable and non-gradable adjectives with intensifiers and softeners

listenings.text: I represent about a dozen artists, and when one of them gets a review, the first thing we both do is look for the adjectives. Not the long paragraphs, the small words in front of the adjectives. Fairly good is not good. Rather interesting is a polite way of saying not interesting enough. And quite is a trap, because quite good means only fairly good, while quite extraordinary means absolutely extraordinary. The review I fear most is not the bad one. A bad review at least means the critic cared. What really hurts an artist is the lukewarm review, the one that calls the work accomplished and thoughtful and then moves on. Nobody remembers it, and nobody goes to the show. When a critic writes absolutely or utterly, good or bad, they have made a decision, and that is the review people read.

The first serious review of my work called it derivative. I was thirty-one, and I read the word on a train and missed my stop. For about a year I told everybody the critic was utterly wrong. Then I went back to the show I had been accused of copying, and I had to admit he was partly right. My early pieces were heavy-handed. I explained everything, so nothing was left for the viewer. What I learned was not to make quieter work, but to trust the audience a little more. Twenty years later another critic called a big installation of mine overrated, and this time I simply asked myself one question. Did it fall flat because the idea was weak, or because the room was wrong? It was the room. That review made the next show better.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: too obvious, explaining everything to the viewer
good in some parts and weak in others
not very enthusiastic, neither positive nor negative
to fail to have the effect that was intended
copying the ideas of other artists, not original
making you think seriously about something
made for the artist's own pleasure, not for the audience

paras: REVIEW A, by Clare Hollis. The Waiting Room is the most ambitious exhibition the Meridian Museum has attempted in a decade, and for the most part it is absolutely extraordinary. Forty artists, six decades and one subject: the hospital, seen from the bed rather than from the doctor's desk. The first room alone is worth the visit. A row of hospital curtains, hung by an artist who spent a year as a cleaner on a cancer ward, is so restrained that you almost walk past it, and then you cannot stop looking.

Not every work is equally accomplished. A few of the video pieces are fairly predictable, and one installation in the final room is rather long. But the best works here are thought-provoking in a way that very few exhibitions about illness manage to be. They do not ask you to feel sorry for anybody. They ask you to notice who is doing the caring, and how little we usually see of them. I left the museum completely exhausted, and I mean that as a compliment.

REVIEW B, by Tom Reyes. Nobody could accuse The Waiting Room of a lack of ambition, and that is exactly its problem. With forty artists and no clear argument, the show is deeply uneven. For every striking work there are three that feel derivative, as if they had been made after a quick visit to a better exhibition. The hospital curtains that other critics have praised are perfectly pleasant, but they are hardly the revelation we have been promised.

The worst moments are heavy-handed. A room of recorded heartbeats, played at full volume, is not moving; it is simply loud. A video in which an artist films herself in a hospital gown for forty minutes is utterly self-indulgent. The idea behind the show is important, and it deserves better than this. Visitors will find some good work here, but the exhibition as a whole is overrated, and its central message falls flat.
